catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbate-giusep: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Giuseppe Baini, born in Rome in 1775 and dead there in 1844, traces the musician's career in the Roman School. Baini trained with his uncle Lorenzo Baini and later with Jannaconi, choirmaster of the Vatican Basilica. Jannaconi brought him into the Sistine Chapel choir as a bass singer. In 1818 Baini was elected its director, a post he held until his death. His works include a ten-voiced Miserere still sung in Holy Week. His lifework, though, was his 1828 memoir of Palestrina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-our-:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Our Lady of Gethsemani describes a Trappist abbey in Nelson County, Kentucky, the first abbey on American soil. On 26 October 1848 a colony of forty Trappists left Melleray in France under Dom Eutrope Proust, reaching New Orleans in early December and travelling by river to Louisville.

Bishop Flaget, who had long wished for their arrival, welcomed them, and on 21 December they took possession of their lands, soon joined by a second colony of twenty from the motherhouse. With indomitable energy the monks cleared the ground and raised an immense quadrilateral, one side formed by the church and the rest by monastic quarters and a guesthouse. A pontifical brief of July 1850 erected the new monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-trin: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on La Trinità di Cava describes a monastery near Cava dei Tirreni, in a gorge of the Finestre hills. Alferio Pappacarbona, a Salerno noble turned Cluniac monk, founded it in 980. Urban the Second endowed it richly, making it subject directly to the Holy See. Boniface the Ninth made it a diocese in 1394, though Leo the Tenth later detached Cava itself, and Cassinese monks replaced the Cluniacs. The abbey holds documents reaching to the 700s, and it now serves as a national school under Benedictine care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-stef:
Agostino Steffani, Spiga's titular bishop, diplomatist, and musician, was born at Castelfranco in Treviso province in 1655. He died at Frankfort in 1728 or 1730. Twelve years old, Count Tattenbach brought him to Munich after hearing him sing at St. Mark's in Venice. At Bavaria's court he stayed twenty-one years, rising from chamber musician to director and court organist.

In 1688 he left Munich for Hanover's court, where he knew Leibniz intimately. In 1698 he settled at Dusseldorf. His compositions fall in three classes. First, religious music, including a Laudate pueri for nine voices and a Psalmodia Vespertina for eight. His Stabat Mater for six with orchestra drew praise that Scarlatti had produced nothing finer. Second, chamber duets, over a hundred preserved and esteemed the most perfect of their kind. Third, operas: five for Munich, nine for Hanover, and at least two for Dusseldorf. Diplomatic missions in 1696 and 1698 suited his gentle, prudent manners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albani:
The Albani were a distinguished Italian family said to descend from Albanian refugees who reached Italy in the fifteenth century. The family soon split into branches at Bergamo and Urbino, and gave the Church one pope, Clement XI, who reigned from 1700 to 1721, along with several well-known cardinals. The entry sketches its leading members one by one, from soldiers and statesmen to churchmen and patrons of learning.

Gian Girolamo of Bergamo, born in 1504, served Venice as a soldier, statesman, and canonist, an expert in church law. Annibale, a cousin of Clement XI, became Cardinal Bishop of Sabina and supported church literature, while his brother Alessandro also rose to the cardinalate. Giovanni Francesco became a cardinal at twenty-seven and later Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. Giuseppe, made cardinal in 1801, sheltered in Vienna from 1796 to 1814 before returning to Rome after Napoleon's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-ma:
Alessandro Manzoni was an Italian poet and novelist, born at Milan in March 1785 and dead there in May 1873. He was the son of Pietro Manzoni, of a feudal family near Lecco, and Giulia, daughter of Cesare Beccaria. After schooling under the Somaschi and the Barnabites and a short stay at Pavia University, he grew up at Milan. His youth mixed study with dissipation. In 1805 he went to live with his mother at Paris, where he took in Voltairean ideas.

In 1808 Manzoni married Henriette-Louise Blondel, a banker's Protestant daughter. When she became Catholic at Paris in 1810, he followed her back into the Church. His creative work of 1812 to 1827 made him the voice of Italian romanticism, defended in his letter On Romanticism. His masterpiece, The Betrothed, dates from 1821 to 1825, with a rewrite in 1840. It tells of two peasants against Spanish oppression in Milan and the war of the Mantuan succession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-pi:
Alessandro Piccolomini was an Italian man of letters, philosopher, and astronomer, born in June 1508 and dead in March 1578. He spent his youth on literature, writing comedies, sonnets, and Italian verse translations of Ovid's Metamorphoses, part of the Aeneid, and Aristotle's Poetics and Rhetoric. He took the Padua chair of philosophy in 1540, writing there on the life of a nobly born man in a free city and on natural philosophy.

In his treatise on the size of the earth and the water, published at Venice in 1558, he fought the Aristotelian and Ptolemaic view. He argued that water does not cover more of the earth than land. The book sparked a controversy with Antonio Berga. In astronomy he held to the Ptolemaic theory, and he also wrote on reforming the calendar in 1578 and on Aristotle's mechanics. Gregory XIII made him titular Bishop of Patras in 1574 and coadjutor at Siena.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-ta:
Alessandro Tassoni was an Italian poet, born at Modena in 1565 and dead there in 1635. He spent his life serving prelates and princes in Italy as secretary or in similar posts. His fame rests chiefly on his mock-heroic poem The Stolen Bucket of 1614. It treats in mock-serious style a mighty struggle between two neighbouring towns over the theft of a well-bucket.

The comic and the serious blend skilfully through the poem, and the methods of ancient epic description are faithfully copied. The work stands with the ancient Battle of the Frogs and Mice, Lope de Vega's Gatomaquia, Boileau's Lutrin, and Pope's Rape of the Lock. Tassoni's dislike of the invading Spaniards shows in his Philippics against the Spaniards. His views on criticism appear in his Considerations on Petrarch's rhymes and his Diverse Thoughts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloisio-garde:
Aloisio Gardellini, born at Rome in 1759 and dead there in 1829, is famous for gathering the decrees of the Congregation of Rites. Before 1587 Mass and the sacraments had obeyed regulations from various popes. In time these grew confused through overlapping, amplification, and abolition. In that year Sixtus V, in the constitution Immensae aeterni Dei, created a body of cardinals, bishops, and clerics to guard proper celebration of the church offices.

A 1730 volume of papal regulations and congregational decrees by the Venetian priest John Baptist Pithonius fell short. Not until 1807 did Gardellini publish the first two volumes of his celebrated collection. A monitum to students of the rites was prefixed. Gardellini was a profound student of the liturgy, unexcelled in diligence, piety, and learning. His collection, comprising all decrees from 1602, grew by three volumes in 1816 and a sixth in 1819, with a few errors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anagni:
Anagni, an Italian diocese in the province of Rome under the direct rule of the Holy See, covers ten towns and claims an apostolic origin. Its bishops enter history in the fifth century. Felix attended the Lateran Synod of 487, and Fortunatus signed the acts of 499. Later bishops won special favour from the popes, among them Zachary, legate at Constantinople in 851 over the election of Photius.

Four popes came from Anagni and were related to one another: Innocent III, Gregory IX, Alexander IV, and Boniface VIII. Thomas Becket found shelter here in flight, and a chapel in the cathedral basement honours him. Boniface VIII was seized here by agents of Philip the Fair. At Anagni too, Alexander III excommunicated the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and renewed the sentence on the antipope Victor IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-spagni:
Andrea Spagni, an educator and author, was born at Florence on 8 August 1716 and died at Rome on 16 September 1788. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1731 and taught philosophy and theology. For a time he taught mathematics at the Roman College and assisted Father Asclepi in astronomical observations.

His most noted work, De Miraculis, published at Rome in 1777 and revised in 1779 and 1785, sets out the doctrine of the nature and reality of miracles. With thoroughness it also gathers the rationalists' objections, from his own and earlier times, against the chief miracles of the Old and New Testaments. It stands as a compendium of the literature up to the last quarter of the eighteenth century. His other works form a Latin series from 1764 to 1781. They cover efficient cause, good, evil, and beauty, the world, the ideas of the human mind, motion, the souls of brutes, and the signs of ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-vanni:
Andrea Vanni, painter and statesman, was born at Siena in 1320 and died in 1414. He entered politics after the democratic overthrow of his city's government. A letter to him from Saint Catherine, his countrywoman and friend, on administration, still survives. He sat on the Grand Council and served as ambassador to the pope at Avignon and to Naples.

As an artist he weakly imitated Simone Martini and Lorenzetti. With Lippo Vanni, Bartolo di Fredi, and Taddeo di Bartolo, he carried Sienese art into the fifteenth century. His work, a polyptych in Santo Stefano at Siena, shows the Virgin enthroned between Stephen, James the Less, John the Baptist, and Bartholomew. Its small heads and gestures show a stiffness. A Madonna and Child in San Michele, a Birth of the Virgin joint with Bartolo di Fredi, and frescoes of Saint Catherine at San Domenico complete his known works. He painted at Naples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-maria-:
Angelo Maria Quirini, called Querini, cardinal and scholar, was born at Venice in 1680 and died at Brescia in 1755. In 1696 he entered the Benedictine order at Florence, becoming professor of Sacred Scripture there in 1705. Five years later he travelled through Germany, the Netherlands, England, and France.

In 1718 the pope put him on the Greek liturgical books commission, and in 1723 named him Bishop of Corfu. A few years later he moved to Brescia as cardinal. He headed the Vatican Library from 1730, later becoming prefect of the Congregation of the Index. He joined the Vienna Academy in 1747, the Berlin Academy in 1748. Opposing fewer holy days brought a controversy with Muratori, ended by Rome in 1750. His Aquileia part brought enforced retirement from Rome in 1751. He gave generously from his own means to German missions. His writings cover Greek liturgy and history, the papacy under Paul II, and an edition of Cardinal Pole's correspondence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-balle:
Born near Bologna in 1805 and dead in Rome in 1881, Antonio Ballerini spent his life as a Jesuit teacher of moral theology. That field is the study of right and wrong conduct in Catholic teaching. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1826 and taught philosophy, church history, and moral theology at Ferentino, Fermo, and the Roman College. He took part in sharp disputes over the writings of Rosmini, the moral system of Alphonsus Liguori, and the ties between bishops and religious orders, above all in England.

His writing also touched the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine that Mary was conceived free from original sin. He helped compile a menology, a calendar of saints' lives, for his order. A short handbook based on Gury reached seminaries in the United States in adapted form. His main work, a commentary on Busenbaum's Medulla, was finished and published by Palmieri after Ballerini's own work on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-marti:
Archbishop of Florence Antonio Martini, born at Prato in 1720 and dead in 1809, is remembered as the scholar behind a modern Italian Bible. After ordination he directed the Superga College at Turin. There Cardinal delle Lanze urged him to meet Pope Benedict XIV's wish for a good version of Scripture in current Tuscan speech. The New Testament, translated from the original Greek, proved too much beside his college duties, so he resigned the directorship for a state council post and pension.

He finished publishing the New Testament in 1771, then worked on the Hebrew Old Testament with help from Rabbi Terni, a Jewish scholar. Pope Pius VI approved the whole work, praised Martini in person, and made him archbishop of Florence in 1781. In that office he partly blocked a garbled edition of his Bible, and a third authorized edition came from his own archiepiscopal press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicae-s:
Apostolicae Sedis Moderationi is a bull of Pius IX, issued 12 October 1869, that recast the system of censures and reserved cases in the Catholic church. It serves in practice as its present penal code. Though the church's founder is divine, its members are human, with human passions, so it needs laws to guide them and penalties to correct them. Over centuries penal statutes piled up, some confirming, some changing, some repealing earlier laws.

The Council of Trent, meeting from 1545 to 1563, simplified them, but new laws then accumulated again until canonists grew confused, moralists perplexed, and the faithful hesitant. Pius IX therefore simplified three hundred years of accumulation in a single bull. The entry explains why a church needs a penal code, how its code grew tangled, and what the 1869 reform set in order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assemani:
Assemani, Arabic Sam'an, or Simeon, is the name of a renowned Maronite family of Mount Lebanon in Syria. Four of its members, all clergy, distinguished themselves in the eighteenth century in East and West. For zeal, learning, and unbounded attachment to Rome, popes held them in great esteem and gave them many well-merited dignities and offices.

Oriental studies, above all Syriac studies, owe them more than any others. Through their research, manuscript collecting, and voluminous publications, Syriac studies and the history, saints' lives, liturgy, and literature of eastern churches were first introduced into Europe. They can justly count, if not as creators, certainly as the most renowned pioneers of modern Oriental studies, preceded by other Maronite scholars known under Latin names such as Echellensis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustino-old:
Augustino Oldoini was an Italian historian and bibliographer, born in 1612, who died at Perugia in 1683. He came from La Spezzia and entered the Society of Jesus in 1628. After the usual studies in humanities, philosophy, and theology, he taught classics at Perugia and then moral philosophy in its theological school. His first work, on hard points of Latin grammar, appeared at Ancona in 1637 while he was teaching humanities.

His later years went to history and bibliography, above all to the popes and cardinals. He prepared a new annotated edition of Ciacconius's History of the Popes, in four volumes issued at Rome between 1670 and 1677, reaching to Clement IX. Around it he published a necrology of popes and antipopes, a work on Clements famed for holiness, and his Roman Athenaeum, a survey of writings by popes, antipopes, and cardinals. He also issued Athenaeums for Perugia and for Liguria in 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-bon:
Balthasar Boncompagni was an Italian mathematician born at Rome in 1821, who died in 1894. His family had given the Church Gregory XIII, reformer of the calendar. He learned mathematics and physics under Santucci and grew into a prolific writer on both subjects and their history. At nineteen he published biographical sketches in the Giornale Arcadico and a paper on definite integrals in Crelle's Journal.

In 1846 the same journal printed his study of physics advances in Italy across the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries. He joined the Accademia dei Lincei in 1847 and soon became its librarian. In 1868 he founded the Bolletino, a journal for the history of mathematics, which he ran until 1887. Its essays covered translators like Gherardo of Cremona and Leonardo, and in 1857 he published a Cambridge manuscript held to translate Al-khwarizmi's arithmetic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barnaba-orian:
Barnaba Oriani was an Italian Barnabite priest who studied the stars, born near Milan in 1752, who died at Milan in 1832. Educated by Barnabites at Milan's San Alessandro College, he joined the order and was ordained at twenty-three. Shortly after, in 1776, he joined the staff of Milan's Brera Observatory, becoming assistant in 1778 and director in 1802. From 1778 he published papers on the stars in the Effemeridi di Milano for fifty-two years.

A 1785 memoir working out Uranus's path won him a high place among star scholars, and he declined Palermo's astronomy chair. He toured Europe's chief star centers at state expense, and under Napoleon refused to swear hatred of monarchy. The government softened his oath, kept him at Brera, and made him head of the weights and measures board. With De Cesaris he measured the arc between Rimini and Rome, and he worked thirty-seven years with Piazzi, who found Ceres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barnabas-of-t:
Barnabas of Terni was a Friar Minor and missionary, of the noble Manassei family, who died in 1474 or 1477. A Doctor of Medicine learned in letters and philosophy, he spurned worldly honors to join the Umbrian Friars Minor. He preached with wonderful success until severe illness stopped him, and served in many offices with prudence and kindness. He zealously promoted the Observance branch of the order.

His lasting honor is founding the first monte di pietà, a charitable loan institution shielding the poor from crushing usury. After consulting the jurist Fortunatus Coppoli and winning wealthy Perugians' support, he opened the first at Perugia in 1462. Violent opposition failed against him at a public disputation, and other cities soon took up the work. Great Franciscan missionaries spread the monti, which wonderfully improved Italy's social conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-battista-guar:
Battista Guarini was an Italian poet born at Ferrara in 1538, who died at Venice in 1612. His father Francesco was a great-grandson of the humanist Guarino da Verona, founder of the family's Ferrara fortunes. After academic years at Padua and Ferrara, he entered Alfonso II's court in 1567 and served as diplomatist, notably in failed bids for Poland's crown in 1574 and 1575.

His domestic life was stormy: his daughter Anna was murdered by her husband with a son's help, and lawsuits embittered his career. His fame rests almost wholly on the Pastor Fido, a lyrical pastoral drama rivaling Tasso's Aminta. Published late in 1589 and often staged, it crowns Italian Renaissance pastoral poetry with shepherds' loves in an imaginary Arcadia. He also wrote lyrics, the comedy Idropica, a dialogue on secretaries, and a treatise backing Medicean Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bellini:
Giacomo Bellini, father of the painters Gentile and Giovanni, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1400 and dead by 1471, he matters most as the teacher who shaped the founders of the Venetian school of painting. His own surviving pictures are few and, by the entry's judgment, minor.

His sketchbook draws the warmer praise, holding copies of ancient statues, Bible scenes, Christian legends, and lively drawings from nature. The entry also sets him against the rival Vivarini painters and notes his work in Venice and beyond. It is a short life of an artist known mainly through his sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-jus:
Benedetto Justiniani, also spelled Giustiniani, was a Jesuit writer on theology and the Bible, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Genoa about 1550, he died at Rome in 1622 after a career spent teaching and preaching. He entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1579 and taught rhetoric and theology in Rome, Toulouse, and Messina.

For more than twenty years he headed the Roman College and served as chief preacher to the pope. Pope Clement VIII also sent him as theologian to Cardinal Cajetan during a mission in Poland. His two great works explain the letters of Paul and the Catholic epistles, and the entry presents them as solid, learned commentaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-men:
Benedetto Menzini, a priest and poet of Florence, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1646 to a poor family, he died at Rome in 1704 after a life spent teaching, writing, and seeking patronage. Early work as a teacher of fine letters led to chairs at Florence and Prato, and later to Rome under Queen Christina of Sweden.

His poems fill the second half of the entry, from heroic odes on Venice and Budapest to elegies, pastoral sonnets, and light lyrics. A poem on the earthly paradise continues Tasso's world, while his satires attack the hollow verse of his day. The entry presents a sharp, learned poet who never quite won the post he wanted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-sest:
Benedict Sestini, a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1816, he died in Maryland in 1890 after a career split between Rome and America. He joined the Jesuits in 1836, studied at the Roman College, and worked as assistant at the Roman Observatory under Father De Vico.

The revolution of 1848 drove him from Rome to Georgetown College, and later to Woodstock, Maryland. His star-colour catalogue, the first broad survey of the heavens by star colour, is his chief scientific work. In later years he also led the Messenger of the Sacred Heart and its prayer league, joining mathematics with devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-lu:
Bernardino Luini, a Milanese painter, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born between 1470 and 1480, perhaps at Luino, he died after 1530. Even his name is unsure: he signed himself Lovinus, and Vasari calls him del Lupino in one place and di Lupino in another. By 1507 he was a master with many commissions.

No proof makes him Leonardo's pupil, though his Virgin and Child pictures and his Christ Crowned with Thorns come very close to Leonardo in colour and feeling. Luini's own mark is sweetness and intense devotion, without Leonardo's mysterious smile or pagan tinge. The entry presents a gentle painter living in a giant's shadow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ippolito-g:
Blessed Ippolito Galantini, founder of Florence's Congregation of Christian Doctrine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1565 to obscure parents, he died in 1619. A childhood cure turned his mind to God's service, and he taught Christian doctrine in the Jesuit church while still a boy.

At twelve he won Archbishop Alexander de' Medici's notice, who gave him the church of Santa Lucia al Prato for his work. Between silk-weaving, his trade, and teaching poor children and adults, he built a congregation of lay catechists. The entry presents a working man turned apostle of Christian teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-colom:
Blessed John Colombini, founder of the Jesuati, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Siena about 1300 to an old patrician family, he died on the road to Acquapendente in 1367. Early life showed no seed of holiness: commerce swelled his fortune, and fellow citizens repeatedly elected him gonfalonier, or chief magistrate.

Avarice marred a fortunate marriage until sickness and grace turned him. He left his luxurious house for a poor hospital ward, then made his home a refuge for the needy, washing their feet with his own hands. Eight years of conversion later he founded the Jesuati, a congregation of lay penitents. The entry presents a merchant turned servant of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-bapti:
Blessed Baptista Varani, an ascetical writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born Camilla Varani at Camerino in 1458, daughter of Duke Julius Caesar Varano and Joanna Malatesta, she died there in 1527. Little is known of her first ten and last twenty-three years; her middle years survive almost entirely through her own writings.

Her confessor, Blessed Peter of Mogliano, drew from her a spiritual autobiography of visions, penance, and devotion to Christ's passion. Entering the Poor Clares, she founded a convent at Camerino and wrote for her sisters. The entry presents a duchess's daughter who wrote her own soul's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-clare:
Blessed Clare of Rimini, of the Poor Clares, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Rimini in 1282, she died there in 1346. Early loss of parents and a pious husband left her exposed to the dangers of youth and beauty. She fell into sinful dissipation. Then a voice at Mass in the Friars Minor church bade her say one Our Father and Hail Mary with fervour.

Reflection followed, and she took the Third Order habit, then founded a convent of Poor Clares, working miracles and growing in contemplation toward life's close. Her body rests in Rimini cathedral, and Pius VI approved her cult in 1782, with a feast on 10 February in city and diocese. The entry presents a sinner turned foundress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonifazio-vit:
Bonifazio Vitalini, a Mantuan jurist turned priest, wrote on criminal law and canon law across a long career. Born at Mantua about 1320, he studied law at Padua and practiced criminal law, publishing his Super maleficis. He then left the law for the priesthood and left Padua, though he came back in 1350 as rector and bishop's vicar.

Two years later he went to Avignon, taught there, and rose through curial offices: prothonotary apostolic, advocate of the consistory, fiscal of the curia, and auditor of the sacred palace. He was still at Avignon in 1388. His works include a commentary on the Clementines and treatises on procedure against apostates and on cases needing a special mandate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brunetto-lati:
Brunetto Latini, Florentine philosopher and statesman, taught Dante and brought oratory and political science into Florentine public life. Born at Florence about 1210, son of Buonaccorso Latini, he worked as a notary and shared in the 1250 revolution that broke Ghibelline power. Sent in 1260 to Alfonso X of Castile for aid against Manfred, he learned on his return that the Guelphs had lost at Montaperti and fled.

At Paris a generous countryman kept him while he studied and worked as notary, and he dedicated his Tresor to that friend. After the Guelph triumph of 1266 he returned to Florence, served as secretary to the Commune, and shaped republican counsels. His French prose Tresor encircles all mortal knowledge, while his earlier Italian Tesoretto, an allegorical poem of Nature, Virtues, Love, and Olympus, plainly influenced Dante, who meets him in Inferno canto fifteen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cajetan-bedin:
Cajetan Bedini, Italian cardinal and diplomat, was born at Sinigaglia on 15 May 1806 and died at Viterbo on 6 September 1864. Pius IX made him Commissary Extraordinary at Bologna in 1849, while revolt shook the Papal Provinces. In 1853, as nuncio to Brazil, he was sent to visit the United States and call on President Franklin Pierce.

His courtesy visit was misread as a bid for diplomatic recognition, and his tour drew anti-Catholic protests throughout, stirred by Italian exiles, the apostate priest Gavazzi, and the Know-Nothings. A plot to kill him failed, and at Cincinnati a plot against him and the cathedral ended in rioting and bloodshed. He left America in January 1854.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camillus-tarq:
Camillus Tarquini, cardinal, Jesuit canonist and archaeologist, was born at Marta on 27 September 1810 and died at Rome on 15 February 1874. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1837, having already published a doctoral thesis on canon law. He held the Roman College chair of canon law, winning notice for his masterly expositions of Scripture at the Gesù.

His treatise on the royal placet for papal bulls, published in 1851 and translated into German, Spanish, and French, forms an appendix to his chief work on public church law of 1862. That work ran through fourteen editions. As an archaeologist he wrote on Etruscan inscriptions, monuments, and language, including an Etruscan grammar and dictionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-goldoni:
Carlo Goldoni was a Venetian dramatist born in February 1707 who died at Paris in January 1793. He remade the Italian theatre by replacing improvised commedia dell'arte with fully worked character plays after Molière, filled with realism drawn from close watch of Italian life. His French Mémoires of 1787 tell his life in detail and recount his fight to improve the repertory against Chiari and Gozzi.

As a boy he followed his physician father through Perugia and Rimini and ran off with a theatrical troupe. He then studied law and served as assistant to a criminal-court clerk at Chioggia. A law degree and advocacy in Venice followed, with playwriting throughout. Later editions of his works ran to 44 volumes in 1795 and 46 volumes in 1817 to 1822, a measure of his standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caroline-book:
The Caroline Books, or Libri Carolini, form a work in four books and some 120 chapters. It claims Charlemagne as author and dates from about 790 to 792. It is a severe critique of the Seventh General Council at Nicaea in 787, above all on sacred images, and a weighty theological treatise in its own right. Both the Iconoclast council of 754 and its opponent, the Second Nicene council, stand judged equally wrong before Frankish criticism.

The first erred, in this judgment, by barring all images as sheer idolatry, while the second erred by urging absolute adoration of images. Learning far beyond Charlemagne's known powers points to another author, perhaps Alcuin or a Spanish or Irish theologian at court. The work grew from a faulty Latin version of the Greek acts. A dropped negative and copyists' slips made the council seem to demand worship of images as of the Trinity itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cavaliere-gio:
Born in Rome in 1571 and dying there in 1644, Baglioni was a painter of distinction, nicknamed the Deaf Man of the Barozzo. His paintings, however, are overshadowed by his biographies of his contemporaries. His chief literary work is his Lives of painters, sculptors, and architects of Rome, covering 1573 to 1642, spanning the reigns from Gregory XIII through Urban VIII.

A pupil of Francesco Morelli, Baglioni painted in Rome for Sixtus V, Clement VIII, and Paul V in turn, working notably in the Vatican, St. Peter's, and St. John Lateran. Paul V honored him with knighthood in the Order of Christ, given for his painting of St. Peter raising Tabitha, now lost. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestino-cav:
Celestino Cavedoni was an Italian ecclesiastic, archaeologist, and numismatist, born at Levizzano-Rangone near Modena on 18 May 1795 and dying at Modena on 26 November 1865. After seminary studies he distinguished himself at Bologna from 1816 to 1821 in archaeology and in Greek and Hebrew. He then became custodian of Modena's numismatic museum and joined the city library, rising to librarian in 1847.

Between 1830 and 1863 he held the hermeneutics chair at the University of Modena. He served as a corresponding member of the commission Napoleon III created to edit the works of Count Borghesi, adding many scientific notes. His numismatic works include studies of Roman family medals, old Italian coin tables, and biblical numismatics, and in 1863 he published a refutation of Renan's Life of Jesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-bianc:
Charles Bianconi was a merchant and philanthropist born in the duchy of Milan in 1785 and dead near Clonmel, Ireland, in 1875. Sent young to Ireland to apprentice with an Italian printseller, he became a wealthy merchant. Between 1815 and 1858 he built the first system of rapid and cheap transport across the whole island. It carried people and government mail. O'Connell counted him an intimate friend, and he promoted Catholic Emancipation, backed many Catholic charities, and supported the Catholic University at Dublin in practical ways.

The English postmaster general reported in 1857 that no living man had done more for the benefit of the sister kingdom. Bianconi showed extraordinary energy and ingenuity in building his vast transport system, increasing his adopted country's resources and knitting its social relations. His Longfield home near Clonmel welcomed guests and served the general welfare in practical ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ri:
The Council of Rimini opened in early July 359 with over four hundred bishops, the Western half of Constantius's twin attempt to settle the Arian strife. An Eastern synod met in parallel. At Rimini, some eighty Semi-Arians withdrew from the orthodox majority, leaving Restitutus of Carthage among its leaders, while exiled Nicene bishops stayed away.

Both parties sent deputations to the emperor. The orthodox professed the faith of Nicaea, while the minority backed the imperial formula drafted by Marcus of Arethusa, which dropped the word essence as unscriptural and divisive. Hasty adoption and lack of papal approval left the result without authority, and Jerome's verdict stands: the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-gino-ca:
This biographical entry follows Count Gino Capponi, a Florentine historian and man of letters born in 1792 and dead in 1876, whose life joined scholarship, travel, and moderate politics. Trained by private tutors in the humanities and in English, French, and German, he travelled widely in Italy and abroad, befriending the exiled poet Foscolo in England.

Back in Florence he helped launch influential periodicals, including the Antologia in 1821 and the Archivio Storico Italiano in 1842, and kept company with the best scholars of his day. In the troubled year 1848 his prudence carried him to head the Grand Duchy's ministry, and he later sat as a senator. Blindness darkened his final years, spent in study and memoir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyril-sieni:
A biographical entry follows Cyril Sieni, better known as Cyril of Barcelona, a Capuchin missionary bishop in Louisiana. Born in Catalonia at an unknown date, he died after 1799. In 1772 the Bishop of Santiago sent him to New Orleans as vicar-general. Louisiana then lay within Santiago's rule.

Church conditions were poor, and the local Capuchin superior had set governor and people against him. As titular Bishop of Tricali and auxiliary of Santiago, Cyril governed seventeen parishes and twenty-one priests across Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, and the Mississippi valley. He sent pastors to Saint Louis, Pensacola, and Saint Augustine. In 1786 he issued a letter on keeping Sunday holy. Despite errors in rule, he was esteemed a holy, simple-minded man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-combon:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Comboni, missionary to Central Africa, born near Brescia in 1831 and dead at Khartoum in 1881. Schooled at Mazza's Institute in Verona, he learned languages and medicine, was ordained in 1854, and first reached Central Africa in 1857 before ill health sent him home in 1859. His 1864 Plan for the Regeneration of Africa launched years of fundraising across Europe.

In 1867 he founded at Verona his Institute for African missions, with a sister institute for women, and opened houses at Cairo to season missionaries for fever country. As pro-vicar apostolic from 1872 and vicar apostolic from 1877, he ruled a vicariate of nearly 100 million souls from just two missions, growing it steadily. He checked the slave trade through the khedive and Sudan's governor, and his institute still carries on his work.

dyke-darrel-the-railroad-detective-or-th:
Dyke Darrel the Railroad Detective, or the Crime of the Midnight Express, by Frank Pinkerton and dated 1886, is a dime novel of train crime. Pinkerton's contents open with a startling crime and the detective's first trick, then introduce Professor Darlington Ruggles. A scalping, a rebuff, and the detective in danger follow at chapter speed, with a handkerchief supplying the clue that turns the case.

Later headings promise a plunge to death, Black Hollow, a burning trap, and Nell missing and in the toils. A baffled villain, a sad fate, and a girl who outmatches the detective himself round out the bill. Railroad detectives were real officers of the new rail corporations, guarding expresses and payrolls, and Pinkerton's hero does that work at melodrama pitch, one chapter ending per cliff edge.
eugenics-and-other-evils-an-argument-aga: Eugenics and Other Evils, G. K. Chesterton's argument against the scientifically organized state. The anti-eugenic polemic. This book preserves that essay. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
forty-centuries-of-ink-or-a-chronologica:
David N. Carvalho spent forty centuries in one book, tracing ink from ancient Egypt to the chemical laboratory. Carvalho marches through classical, medieval, and Renaissance inks, then studies recipes, classifications, and the utensils of writing, from reed pens and quills to steel nibs and pencils. Papyrus, parchment, vellum, and true paper get chapters as ink's backgrounds, the surfaces it sits on.

The last part turns legal: official ink, enduring ink, fraudulent ink, and chemico-legal ink, meaning ink tested as courtroom evidence. Carvalho warns that most modern inks fade fast, a danger to records. History, chemistry, anecdotes, and poetry crowd together in an enthusiast's survey of a humble substance.
govdocs-archive_org-nihilism-franco-volp:
Franco Volpi, an Italian philosopher, wrote Nihilism as a history of one of philosophy's darkest concepts. He develops an earlier synopsis of the problem into a full account, following nihilism from its roots in German idealism onward.

The story runs through Nietzsche, who named nihilism as Europe's coming crisis, and into the twentieth century, where the collapse of old values became a central theme of thought. Volpi writes as a historian of ideas, tracing who used the word and what each meant by it. The book suits readers of continental philosophy who want the concept's whole career.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CommunistInvolv:
On June 9, 1964, the FBI's San Francisco office sent this confidential memorandum concerning Lee Harvey Oswald. It belongs to the Bureau's Oswald file at the height of the Warren Commission's work, when every office's holdings on the accused assassin were being gathered and summarized.

The archive's filing label ties the memo to the question of alleged Communist involvement. That was the charge the Bureau had tracked since Oswald's defection to the Soviet Union in 1959 and his return with a Russian wife. Memos of this kind weighed his Marxism, his contacts, and his committees. The single memo is preserved as a page of the Bureau's political file on Oswald.

The charge ties a respected university to the machinery of empire. Training programs look neutral on a catalog page, and Petran asks readers to see the politics inside them. Her article preserves a sharp left critique of how American power staffed itself after the war.
govdocs-archive_org-the-mystery-of-the-h: Luis Felipe Moyano Cires, writing as Nimrod de Rosario, cast his teaching as a magical novel, The Mystery of Belicena Villca. madame-firmiani:
Madame Firmiani is a short tale by Honoré de Balzac, in Katharine Wormeley's translation. Balzac dedicated it to his old friend Alexandre de Berny. His opening pages muse on stories that only the heart can tell. Some portraits, he says, need an infusion of soul to live.

Madame Firmiani is a beautiful widow at the center of Paris gossip. A young man loves her, while rumors say her fortune is ruined. Balzac peels away the world's false account of her. Her true story proves nobler and sadder than the talk. The tale belongs to his great Human Comedy. It glitters with Parisian air and quiet moral force.
massimilla-doni:
Honore de Balzac wrote Massimilla Doni, here in English by Clara Bell and James Waring. A note to Jacques Strunz opens the book. Balzac thanks Strunz for teaching him the craft behind fine music.

Venice fills the first pages, with its old and proud noble houses. Balzac says that glory has sunk into ruin and want. Gondoliers now serve the English, though some bear names older than kings. Love and opera grow from that rich, faded ground. Balzac's note admits his guide knew far more of music than he did. That debt shapes the tale's deep care for song and stage.
nasa-tm-19660021864-asee-university-of-m:

pausanias-the-spartan-the-haunted-and-th:
Pausanias, the Spartan is an unfinished historical romance by Edward Bulwer-Lytton, edited after his death by his son. The son's dedication letter explains that Lytton began the work fifteen or twenty years earlier and kept returning to it. The subject haunted his imagination and was never abandoned.

Pausanias, regent of Sparta, built a vast conspiracy known only in brief from Thucydides and Plutarch. Had it succeeded, his son notes, it would have changed history. The volume pairs the fragment with Lytton's ghost story "The Haunted and the Haunters," two works from opposite ends of his art.

schiller-wallenstein-coleridge-1800-picc:
S T Coleridge's translation of Schiller's Wallenstein, Part 1: The Piccolomini, appeared in 1800. Friedrich Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy was the great German historical drama of its age. Coleridge, the English poet, translated two parts during his stay in Germany and made them his own in English verse.

The Piccolomini sets the stage in the Thirty Years' War, where General Wallenstein's army waits and wonders at his plans. Young Max Piccolomini loves Wallenstein's daughter while his father plots against the general. Loyalty, ambition, and star lore hang over the camp scenes. Coleridge's version was a turning point for English Romantic drama, proof that German theater could live in English.
the-concept-of-nature-the-tarner-lecture:
Alfred North Whitehead delivered these lectures at Trinity College in November 1919, as the first course of Tarner lectures. A transcriber's note explains the handling of mathematical notation, with carets for superscripts, underscores for subscripts, and Greek letters written out. Two printer's errors, the note adds, have been corrected by sense.

Whitehead's preface explains the lectureship itself. It is an occasional office founded by the generosity of Mr. Edward Tarner. Each holder's duty is to deliver a course on the philosophy of the sciences and the relations between them, as the preface begins to state. Whitehead's course takes the concept of nature as its theme. That means asking what nature is as an object of thought, apart from the mind that thinks it. The lectures became a landmark in his philosophy, and the plain preface, with its thanks to the founder, sets the formal frame for a demanding argument.

un-un-res-report-of-the-secretary-genera:
Ground rules for the United Nations Emergency Force in Egypt are laid down in this 1956 report of the Secretary-General, document A/3375. The force was the first of its kind, sent during the Suez Crisis to stand between armies. Egypt's consent, and clear limits on the force, were the price of its welcome.

The report states that the force would enter only with Egypt's agreement and would not fight except in self-defense. It covers freedom of movement, ties to local authorities, and the force's neutral role. These basic points became core doctrine for peacekeeping around the world.
zanoni:
Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote this occult novel, framed here by his 1845 dedicatory letter to sculptor John Gibson. Lytton praises Gibson for living apart from rivalry and greed. Gibson works in Rome among the loveliest remains of the past, he writes. Fame without a desire for gold marks the true artist. That ideal, Lytton says, matches the principle the novel seeks to convey.

The letter sets a high, serious tone before the tale begins. Hidden wisdom and spiritual aspiration drive Zanoni's story of an immortal adept. Readers get Rosicrucian mystery mixed with love and sacrifice. Lytton's praise of Canova's pupil also preserves a glimpse of Rome's art world.
